items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix [MATH: M\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: x − y + z = 6; y − 3z = − 13; − x − y − z = − 4]

Content:
We can reduce [MATH: M] to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of [MATH: 2 \times 2] systems.

Content:
Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of [MATH: 1]'s with [MATH: 0]'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: M|∼[1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; − 1|− 1|− 1|− 4]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + R_{1}; ∼[1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; 0|− 2|0|2]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + 2R_{2}; ∼[1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; 0|0|− 6|− 24]|R_{3}|:= − (1)/(6)R_{3}; ∼[1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; 0|0|1|4].]

Content:
The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

Content:
Note: The row echelon form of a matrix is not unique. In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

Content:
[MATH: 1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; 0|0|− 6|− 24]

Content:
This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain [MATH: 1]'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

Content:
[MATH: 1|− 1|1|6; 0|1|− 3|− 13; 0|0|1|4]

Content:
Having [MATH: 1]'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

  2. We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below [MATH: a_{11}] equal to [MATH: 0.] Namely,

    • if [MATH: a_{21} eq 0,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;]

    • if [MATH: a_{31} eq 0,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.]

  3. If [MATH: a_{22} eq 1,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.]

  4. We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below [MATH: a_{22}] equal to [MATH: 0.] Namely,

The standard Gaussian elimination for a [MATH: 3 \times 3] system can be described as follows:

1. If [MATH: a_{11} \neq 0] and [MATH: a_{11} \neq 1,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.]
2. We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below [MATH: a_{11}] equal to [MATH: 0.] Namely,

- if [MATH: a_{21} \neq 0,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;]
- if [MATH: a_{31} \neq 0,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.]
3. If [MATH: a_{22} \neq 1,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.]
4. We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below [MATH: a_{22}] equal to [MATH: 0.] Namely,

- if [MATH: a_{32} \neq 0,] then we use the row operation [MATH: R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.]

Consider the system of linear equations

[MATH: x − y + z = 1; y + z = − 2; − x + 2y + z = − 1.]

sections.readable_text:
Consider the system of linear equations

[MATH: x − y + z = 1; y + z = − 2; − x + 2y + z = − 1.]

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Reducing [MATH: M] to row echelon form, we have

[MATH: M|∼[1|− 1|1|1; 0|1|1|− 2; − 1|2|1|− 1]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + R_{1}; ∼[1|− 1|1|1; 0|1|1|− 2; 0|1|2|0]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− 1)R_{2}; ∼[1|− 1|1|1; 0|1|1|− 2; 0|0|1|2].]

The system is now [MATH: x − y + z = 1; y + z = − 2; z = 2,]

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation [MATH: z=2] tells us the value of [MATH: z.] Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

[MATH: y + (2) = − 2⟹y = − 4.]

Finally, substituting both [MATH: y=-4] and [MATH: z=2] into the first equation, we get [MATH: x − (− 4) + (2) = 1⟹x = − 5.]

Therefore, the solution is [MATH: x=-5,] [MATH: y=-4,] and [MATH: z=2.] Or, in vector form, [MATH: \langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:

[MATH: 1|1|1|− 2; 1|1|2|− 1; 1|2|1|1]

Reducing [MATH: M] to row echelon form, we have

[MATH: M|∼[1|1|1|− 2; 1|1|2|− 1; 1|2|1|1]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|0|1|1; 1|2|1|1]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|0|1|1; 0|1|0|3].]

Note that we get [MATH: a_{22}=0.] Therefore, we swap the [MATH: 2]nd and [MATH: 3]rd rows: [MATH: M|∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|0|1|1; 0|1|0|3]|R_{2}|↔R_{3}; ∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|1|0|3; 0|0|1|1]]

The system is now [MATH: x + y + z = − 2; y = 3; z = 1,]

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation [MATH: z=1] tells us the value of [MATH: z,] and the second equation [MATH: y=3] tells us the value of [MATH: y.] Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

[MATH: x + (3) + (1) = − 2⟹x = − 6.]

Therefore, the solution is [MATH: x=-6,] [MATH: y=3,] and [MATH: z=1.] Or, in vector form, [MATH: \langle -6,3,1 \rangle.]

The augmented matrix for this system is

[MATH: M|∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|0|1|1; 0|1|0|3]|R_{2}|↔R_{3}; ∼[1|1|1|− 2; 0|1|0|3; 0|0|1|1]]

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation [MATH: z=1] tells us the value of [MATH: z,] and the second equation [MATH: y=3] tells us the value of [MATH: y.] Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

[MATH: x + (3) + (1) = − 2⟹x = − 6.]
